q: What does ELB stand for in AWS?

exp.a: Correct. ELB stands for Elastic Load Balancer, a managed AWS service that distributes incoming traffic across multiple targets.
exp.b: Incorrect. There is no AWS service called Enhanced Load Balancer.
exp.c: Incorrect. Broadcasting is not a term used in this context.
exp.d: Incorrect. ELB is not called External Load Balancer.

q: What does ASG stand for in AWS?

exp.a: Incorrect. Security Groups are a separate concept in AWS.
exp.b: Correct. ASG stands for Auto Scaling Group, which automatically adjusts the number of EC2 instances based on demand.
exp.c: Incorrect. There is no service called Automated Server Group.
exp.d: Incorrect. There is no service called Application Scaling Gateway.

q: How many types of Elastic Load Balancers does AWS currently offer?

exp.a: Incorrect. AWS offers more than 2 types of load balancers.
exp.b: Incorrect. AWS offers 4 types: CLB, ALB, NLB, and GWLB.
exp.c: Correct. AWS offers 4 types: Classic Load Balancer (CLB), Application Load Balancer (ALB), Network Load Balancer (NLB), and Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB).
exp.d: Incorrect. AWS currently offers 4 types of load balancers.

q: At which OSI layer does the Application Load Balancer (ALB) operate?

exp.a: Incorrect. Layer 3 is the Network layer, which deals with IP routing.
exp.b: Incorrect. Layer 4 is the Transport layer where NLB operates.
exp.c: Incorrect. Layer 5 is the Session layer.
exp.d: Correct. ALB operates at Layer 7 (Application layer) and can route based on HTTP/HTTPS content like URL paths, headers, and query strings.

q: At which OSI layer does the Network Load Balancer (NLB) operate?

exp.a: Correct. NLB operates at Layer 4 (Transport layer) and handles TCP, UDP, and TLS traffic.
exp.b: Incorrect. Layer 5 is the Session layer.
exp.c: Incorrect. Layer 6 is the Presentation layer.
exp.d: Incorrect. Layer 7 is where ALB operates.

q: What is the primary purpose of an Elastic Load Balancer?

opts.a: To store data in the cloud
opts.b: To distribute incoming traffic across multiple targets

exp.a: Incorrect. Data storage is handled by services like S3 and EBS.
exp.b: Correct. ELB distributes incoming application traffic across multiple targets such as EC2 instances, containers, and IP addresses.
exp.c: Incorrect. Encryption at rest is handled by KMS and other encryption services.
exp.d: Incorrect. Monitoring logs is handled by CloudWatch and CloudTrail.

q: Which load balancer type is best suited for handling millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency?

exp.a: Incorrect. CLB is a legacy load balancer and not optimized for ultra-low latency at scale.
exp.b: Incorrect. ALB operates at Layer 7 and has higher latency compared to NLB.
exp.c: Correct. NLB is designed to handle millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency (~100ms vs ~400ms for ALB).
exp.d: Incorrect. GWLB is designed for third-party virtual appliances, not for ultra-low latency traffic distribution.

q: Which ELB type supports static IP addresses and Elastic IP addresses?

exp.a: Incorrect. ALB does not support static or Elastic IP addresses directly.
exp.b: Incorrect. CLB does not support Elastic IP addresses.
exp.c: Correct. NLB provides a static IP per Availability Zone and supports assigning Elastic IP addresses.
exp.d: Incorrect. GWLB does not provide static IP addresses for client-facing use.

q: What is the minimum number of Availability Zones recommended for an ELB?

exp.a: Incorrect. Using only 1 AZ does not provide high availability.
exp.b: Correct. AWS recommends at least 2 Availability Zones for high availability when configuring an ELB.
exp.c: Incorrect. While 3 AZs provide even better availability, the minimum recommendation is 2.
exp.d: Incorrect. 4 AZs are not the minimum requirement.

q: What is the purpose of health checks in ELB?

opts.b: To verify that registered targets are healthy and can receive traffic
opts.c: To scale instances up or down

exp.a: Incorrect. Encryption is handled by SSL/TLS certificates, not health checks.
exp.b: Correct. Health checks verify the health of registered targets and ELB only sends traffic to healthy targets.
exp.c: Incorrect. Scaling is handled by Auto Scaling Groups.
exp.d: Incorrect. Logging is handled by access logs, not health checks.

q: On which port does a default HTTP health check operate?

exp.a: Incorrect. Port 22 is used for SSH.
exp.b: Incorrect. Port 443 is used for HTTPS.
exp.c: Correct. The default HTTP health check operates on port 80.
exp.d: Incorrect. Port 3389 is used for RDP (Windows Remote Desktop).

q: What HTTP status code indicates a healthy target in an ELB health check?

exp.a: Incorrect. 100 is a Continue status code.
exp.b: Correct. HTTP 200 (OK) indicates the target is healthy.
exp.c: Incorrect. 302 is a redirect status code and does not indicate a healthy target by default.
exp.d: Incorrect. 500 is an Internal Server Error and indicates an unhealthy target.

q: Which feature of ALB allows routing based on URL path?

exp.a: Incorrect. Sticky sessions bind a user's session to a specific target.
exp.b: Correct. Path-based routing allows ALB to route requests to different target groups based on the URL path (e.g., /api, /images).
exp.c: Incorrect. Cross-zone load balancing distributes traffic evenly across all registered targets in all enabled AZs.
exp.d: Incorrect. Connection draining allows in-flight requests to complete before deregistering a target.

q: What is the default health check interval for ELB?

exp.a: Incorrect. 10 seconds is not the default interval.
exp.b: Correct. The default health check interval is 30 seconds.
exp.c: Incorrect. 60 seconds is not the default interval.
exp.d: Incorrect. 5 seconds is not the default interval for standard health checks.

q: Which AWS service does Auto Scaling Group use to launch new instances?

exp.a: Incorrect. CloudFormation is an infrastructure-as-code service.
exp.b: Correct. ASG uses Launch Templates (or the older Launch Configurations) to define how new EC2 instances should be launched.
exp.c: Incorrect. Lambda is a serverless compute service.
exp.d: Incorrect. Elastic Beanstalk is a PaaS service that may use ASG internally but is not what ASG directly uses.

q: What are the three main capacity settings in an Auto Scaling Group?

exp.a: Correct. ASG has three key capacity settings: Minimum (minimum number of instances), Maximum (maximum number of instances), and Desired (target number of instances).
exp.b: Incorrect. These are actions, not capacity settings.
exp.c: Incorrect. These are not ASG capacity parameters.
exp.d: Incorrect. These are not ASG capacity parameters.

q: If an ASG has minimum capacity of 2, desired capacity of 4, and maximum capacity of 6, how many instances will be running under normal conditions?

exp.a: Incorrect. 2 is the minimum, but under normal conditions ASG maintains the desired capacity.
exp.b: Correct. Under normal conditions, ASG maintains the desired capacity which is 4 instances.
exp.c: Incorrect. 6 is the maximum capacity and is only reached during peak demand.
exp.d: Incorrect. 3 is not any of the configured capacity values.

q: Which scaling policy adjusts capacity based on a target metric value (e.g., keep average CPU at 50%)?

exp.a: Incorrect. Simple scaling adds or removes a fixed number of instances based on a single alarm.
exp.b: Incorrect. Step scaling adjusts capacity in steps based on the size of the alarm breach.
exp.c: Correct. Target Tracking Scaling automatically adjusts the number of instances to keep a specified metric at a target value (e.g., maintain average CPU utilization at 50%).
exp.d: Incorrect. Scheduled scaling adjusts capacity based on a predefined schedule.

q: Which scaling policy allows you to scale based on a known traffic pattern at specific times?

exp.a: Incorrect. Target tracking adjusts based on real-time metrics, not predefined times.
exp.b: Incorrect. Predictive scaling uses machine learning to forecast demand, not fixed schedules.
exp.c: Correct. Scheduled scaling allows you to set specific times to scale in or out based on known traffic patterns (e.g., scale up at 9 AM on weekdays).
exp.d: Incorrect. Simple scaling reacts to CloudWatch alarms, not schedules.

q: What is the default cooldown period for an Auto Scaling Group?

exp.a: Incorrect. 60 seconds is not the default cooldown period.
exp.b: Incorrect. 120 seconds is not the default cooldown period.
exp.c: Correct. The default cooldown period is 300 seconds (5 minutes), during which ASG will not launch or terminate additional instances.
exp.d: Incorrect. 600 seconds is not the default cooldown period.

q: What is Cross-Zone Load Balancing?

opts.a: Balancing traffic between different AWS regions
opts.b: Distributing traffic evenly across all registered targets in all enabled Availability Zones
opts.c: Routing traffic to the nearest AWS edge location

exp.a: Incorrect. Cross-zone load balancing works within a single region across AZs.
exp.b: Correct. Cross-zone load balancing ensures that traffic is distributed evenly across all registered instances in all enabled Availability Zones, regardless of which AZ the traffic enters.
exp.c: Incorrect. Edge location routing is done by CloudFront.
exp.d: Incorrect. Encryption between zones is not what cross-zone load balancing does.

q: Is Cross-Zone Load Balancing enabled by default for Application Load Balancer?

opts.a: Yes, and it cannot be disabled
opts.b: Yes, and it can be disabled at the target group level
opts.c: No, it must be enabled manually
opts.d: No, ALB does not support cross-zone load balancing

exp.a: Incorrect. It is enabled by default but can be disabled at the target group level.
exp.b: Correct. For ALB, cross-zone load balancing is enabled by default and can be disabled at the target group level. There are no charges for inter-AZ data with ALB.
exp.c: Incorrect. It is enabled by default for ALB.
exp.d: Incorrect. ALB supports cross-zone load balancing.

q: Is Cross-Zone Load Balancing enabled by default for Network Load Balancer?

opts.c: No, it is disabled by default
opts.d: NLB does not support cross-zone load balancing

exp.a: Incorrect. It is not enabled by default for NLB.
exp.b: Incorrect. It is disabled by default for NLB.
exp.c: Correct. For NLB, cross-zone load balancing is disabled by default. If enabled, you pay charges for inter-AZ data transfer.
exp.d: Incorrect. NLB does support cross-zone load balancing.

q: What is the purpose of sticky sessions (session affinity) in ELB?

opts.b: To ensure a client is always directed to the same target instance
opts.c: To distribute traffic equally across all targets

exp.a: Incorrect. Encryption is handled by SSL/TLS, not sticky sessions.
exp.b: Correct. Sticky sessions ensure that requests from the same client are always routed to the same target instance using cookies.
exp.c: Incorrect. Equal distribution is the default behavior without sticky sessions.
exp.d: Incorrect. Idle connection termination is related to idle timeout settings.

q: Which types of cookies are used for sticky sessions in ALB?

exp.a: Incorrect. These are general cookie types, not specific to ALB sticky sessions.
exp.b: Correct. ALB supports application-based cookies (custom or generated by the load balancer with name AWSALBAPP) and duration-based cookies (generated by the load balancer with name AWSALB).
exp.c: Incorrect. These are general web cookie classifications.
exp.d: Incorrect. These are not the types used for ALB sticky sessions.

q: What is Connection Draining (called Deregistration Delay in ALB/NLB)?

opts.a: Immediately terminating all connections when an instance is removed
opts.b: Allowing in-flight requests to complete while the instance is being deregistered
opts.c: Draining the CPU resources of an instance
opts.d: Removing all data from an instance before termination

exp.a: Incorrect. Connection draining does the opposite — it allows existing connections to finish.
exp.b: Correct. Connection Draining / Deregistration Delay gives in-flight requests time to complete on instances that are being deregistered or marked unhealthy.
exp.c: Incorrect. CPU draining is not a concept in this context.
exp.d: Incorrect. Data removal is not related to connection draining.

q: What is the default deregistration delay (connection draining) value?

exp.a: Incorrect. 60 seconds is not the default value.
exp.b: Correct. The default deregistration delay is 300 seconds (5 minutes). It can be set between 0 and 3600 seconds.
exp.c: Incorrect. 600 seconds is not the default value.
exp.d: Incorrect. 3600 seconds is the maximum value, not the default.

q: What is SSL/TLS termination in the context of ELB?

opts.b: Decrypting incoming SSL/TLS traffic at the load balancer before forwarding to targets

exp.a: Incorrect. SSL termination does not block encrypted traffic.
exp.b: Correct. SSL/TLS termination means the ELB decrypts the incoming encrypted traffic and forwards it to backend targets, reducing the encryption burden on instances.
exp.c: Incorrect. Creating certificates is done via AWS Certificate Manager (ACM).
exp.d: Incorrect. This has nothing to do with terminating instances.

q: Which AWS service is used to manage SSL/TLS certificates for ELB?

exp.a: Incorrect. KMS manages encryption keys, not SSL certificates.
exp.b: Correct. AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) is used to provision, manage, and deploy SSL/TLS certificates for use with ELB.
exp.c: Incorrect. Secrets Manager stores secrets like database credentials, not SSL certificates for ELB.
exp.d: Incorrect. IAM manages user permissions, not SSL certificates (though IAM can store certificates, ACM is the recommended service).

q: What is Server Name Indication (SNI)?

opts.a: A protocol that assigns static IPs to servers
opts.b: A method that allows multiple SSL certificates on one load balancer to serve multiple domains

exp.a: Incorrect. SNI does not assign static IPs.
exp.b: Correct. SNI allows a load balancer to host multiple TLS certificates for different domains. The client indicates the hostname during the TLS handshake, and the server selects the appropriate certificate.
exp.c: Incorrect. DNS routing is managed by Route 53.
exp.d: Incorrect. SNI is not a health check mechanism.

q: Which ELB types support Server Name Indication (SNI)?

exp.a: Incorrect. CLB does not support SNI — it only supports one SSL certificate.
exp.b: Correct. Only ALB and NLB support SNI, allowing multiple SSL certificates for multiple domains.
exp.c: Incorrect. CLB does not support SNI.
exp.d: Incorrect. GWLB does not handle SSL termination.

q: What protocol does the Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) use?

exp.a: Incorrect. GWLB does not use HTTP.
exp.b: Incorrect. While GWLB operates at Layer 3, it uses the GENEVE protocol.
exp.c: Correct. GWLB uses the GENEVE protocol on port 6081 to encapsulate and forward traffic to third-party virtual appliances.
exp.d: Incorrect. GWLB does not use UDP on port 443.

q: At which OSI layer does the Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) operate?

exp.a: Correct. GWLB operates at Layer 3 (Network layer) and deals with IP packets.
exp.b: Incorrect. Layer 4 is where NLB operates.
exp.c: Incorrect. No ELB operates at Layer 5.
exp.d: Incorrect. Layer 7 is where ALB operates.

q: What is the primary use case for Gateway Load Balancer?

opts.a: Distributing web traffic to EC2 instances
opts.b: Deploying, scaling, and managing third-party virtual appliances (firewalls, IDS/IPS)

exp.a: Incorrect. Web traffic distribution is handled by ALB or NLB.
exp.b: Correct. GWLB is used to deploy, scale, and manage third-party network virtual appliances like firewalls, intrusion detection/prevention systems.
exp.c: Incorrect. Caching is handled by CloudFront or ElastiCache.
exp.d: Incorrect. DNS management is handled by Route 53.

q: Which ALB feature allows routing based on the hostname in the request?

exp.a: Incorrect. Path-based routing routes based on URL path, not hostname.
exp.b: Correct. Host-based routing allows ALB to route requests to different target groups based on the Host header (e.g., api.example.com vs www.example.com).
exp.c: Incorrect. IP-based routing is not a standard ALB routing rule type name.
exp.d: Incorrect. Geo-based routing is a Route 53 feature.

q: What is a Target Group in the context of ALB/NLB?

opts.a: A security group for the load balancer
opts.b: A logical grouping of targets (EC2 instances, IP addresses, Lambda functions) that receive traffic

exp.a: Incorrect. Security groups and target groups are different concepts.
exp.b: Correct. A target group is a logical grouping of targets (such as EC2 instances, IP addresses, or Lambda functions) where the load balancer routes requests.
exp.c: Incorrect. IAM user groups are unrelated to ELB.
exp.d: Incorrect. S3 buckets are not part of ELB target groups.

q: Which of the following can be a target in an ALB target group?

opts.a: EC2 instances, IP addresses, Lambda functions, and other ALBs

exp.a: Correct. ALB target groups can contain EC2 instances, IP addresses (including private IPs), Lambda functions, and even other ALBs.
exp.b: Incorrect. ALB supports more target types than just EC2 instances.
exp.c: Incorrect. IP addresses are one of several supported target types.
exp.d: Incorrect. Lambda functions are one of several supported target types.

q: What happens when all instances in a target group are unhealthy?

opts.b: ELB routes traffic to all targets regardless of health status (fail-open)
opts.d: ELB redirects to a different region

exp.a: Incorrect. ELB does not completely stop traffic in this scenario.
exp.b: Correct. When all targets in a target group are unhealthy, ELB will route requests to all targets (fail-open behavior) as a last resort.
exp.c: Incorrect. ELB does not create instances; that is the role of ASG.
exp.d: Incorrect. ELB does not redirect to other regions automatically.

q: What is the purpose of the X-Forwarded-For header in ELB?

opts.b: To identify the original client IP address when traffic passes through the load balancer

exp.a: Incorrect. X-Forwarded-For does not encrypt requests.
exp.b: Correct. X-Forwarded-For header contains the original client's IP address since the backend instance sees the ELB's private IP as the source.
exp.c: Incorrect. Target selection is done by the load balancer's routing algorithm.
exp.d: Incorrect. Cookie expiration is unrelated to X-Forwarded-For.

q: Which header does ALB add to indicate the protocol (HTTP or HTTPS) used by the client?

exp.a: Incorrect. X-Forwarded-For contains the client's IP address.
exp.b: Correct. X-Forwarded-Proto indicates the protocol (HTTP or HTTPS) that the client used to connect to the load balancer.
exp.c: Incorrect. X-Forwarded-Port indicates the port used by the client.
exp.d: Incorrect. X-Forwarded-Host is not a standard ALB header.

q: What is the default idle timeout for an Application Load Balancer?

exp.a: Incorrect. 30 seconds is not the default idle timeout for ALB.
exp.b: Correct. The default idle timeout for ALB is 60 seconds. If no data is sent over a connection for 60 seconds, the load balancer closes the connection.
exp.c: Incorrect. 120 seconds is not the default.
exp.d: Incorrect. 300 seconds is not the default idle timeout.

q: Which type of Auto Scaling policy uses machine learning to forecast future traffic and pre-scales?

exp.a: Incorrect. Target tracking adjusts based on current metric values.
exp.b: Incorrect. Step scaling responds to alarm breaches with predefined steps.
exp.c: Correct. Predictive Scaling uses machine learning to analyze historical traffic patterns and forecast future demand, proactively scaling ahead of anticipated load.
exp.d: Incorrect. Scheduled scaling uses fixed time-based rules.

q: What metric is commonly used for Target Tracking Scaling in ASG?

exp.a: Incorrect. Disk read operations are not commonly used for target tracking scaling.
exp.b: Correct. Average CPU Utilization (e.g., keep at 40-50%) is one of the most commonly used metrics for target tracking scaling. Other common metrics include Average Network In/Out and ALBRequestCountPerTarget.
exp.c: Incorrect. S3 object count is unrelated to ASG scaling.
exp.d: Incorrect. IAM user count is unrelated to ASG scaling.

q: What is the minimum value you can set for ASG minimum capacity?

exp.a: Correct. The minimum capacity of an ASG can be set to 0, meaning no instances run when there is no demand.
exp.b: Incorrect. While 1 is a common setting, the minimum can be 0.
exp.c: Incorrect. 2 is not the minimum value you can set.
exp.d: Incorrect. 3 is not the minimum value you can set.

q: Which scaling type in ASG adds or removes instances in response to CloudWatch alarms?

exp.a: Incorrect. Manual scaling requires human intervention to change capacity.
exp.b: Correct. Dynamic Scaling (which includes Simple, Step, and Target Tracking policies) reacts to CloudWatch alarms to automatically add or remove instances.
exp.c: Incorrect. Scheduled scaling acts on predefined schedules, not alarms.
exp.d: Incorrect. Predictive scaling uses ML forecasts, not alarms.

q: What is the default termination policy for Auto Scaling Groups?

opts.b: Terminate the instance with the oldest launch configuration/template, then the one closest to the next billing hour
opts.d: Terminate the instance with highest CPU usage

exp.a: Incorrect. ASG does not terminate the newest instance by default.
exp.b: Correct. The default termination policy first selects the AZ with the most instances, then terminates the instance with the oldest launch configuration/template, and among those, the one closest to the next billing hour.
exp.c: Incorrect. ASG does not terminate randomly by default.
exp.d: Incorrect. CPU usage is not used in the default termination policy.

q: What is the warm-up period in the context of ASG scaling?

opts.a: Time for an instance to boot the operating system
opts.b: Time allowed for a newly launched instance to stabilize before it contributes to CloudWatch metrics
opts.c: Time before the ASG is deleted

exp.a: Incorrect. OS boot time is part of it, but warm-up includes application readiness.
exp.b: Correct. The warm-up period is the time a newly launched instance needs before its metrics are included in scaling calculations, preventing premature scaling actions.
exp.c: Incorrect. ASG deletion is unrelated to warm-up.
exp.d: Incorrect. DNS propagation is unrelated to instance warm-up.

q: Which ELB type was the first to be offered by AWS and is now considered legacy?

exp.a: Incorrect. ALB was introduced in 2016.
exp.b: Incorrect. NLB was introduced in 2017.
exp.c: Correct. Classic Load Balancer (CLB) was the first ELB offered by AWS (2009) and is now considered legacy. AWS recommends using ALB or NLB instead.
exp.d: Incorrect. GWLB was introduced in 2020.

q: What is the maximum number of listeners you can create per Application Load Balancer?

exp.a: Incorrect. The limit is higher than 10.
exp.b: Incorrect. The limit is higher than 25.
exp.c: Correct. You can configure up to 50 listeners per Application Load Balancer.
exp.d: Incorrect. The default limit is 50 listeners per ALB.

q: How many rules can be configured per ALB listener (excluding the default rule)?

exp.a: Incorrect. 10 is too few.
exp.b: Incorrect. 50 is not the correct limit.
exp.c: Correct. You can configure up to 100 rules per ALB listener (excluding the default rule).
exp.d: Incorrect. 200 exceeds the default limit.

q: What is the maximum number of target groups per ALB?

exp.a: Incorrect. 10 is not the correct limit.
exp.b: Incorrect. 50 is not the correct limit.
exp.c: Correct. By default, you can have up to 100 target groups per Application Load Balancer.
exp.d: Incorrect. 200 exceeds the default limit.

q: Which feature allows ALB to authenticate users before forwarding requests to targets?

exp.a: Incorrect. WAF protects against web exploits but doesn't authenticate users.
exp.b: Correct. ALB supports native authentication via OIDC and integration with Amazon Cognito, allowing user authentication before traffic reaches your application.
exp.c: Incorrect. Security groups filter traffic but don't authenticate users.
exp.d: Incorrect. NACLs are network-level access controls, not authentication mechanisms.

q: What is the NLB latency approximately?

exp.a: Incorrect. ~400ms is the approximate latency for ALB.
exp.b: Correct. NLB provides ultra-low latency of approximately 100 milliseconds (compared to ~400ms for ALB).
exp.c: Incorrect. 1 second would be very high latency for a load balancer.
exp.d: Incorrect. 10ms is lower than NLB's typical latency.

q: What is the ALB latency approximately?

exp.a: Incorrect. 50ms is lower than ALB's typical latency.
exp.b: Incorrect. ~100ms is the approximate NLB latency.
exp.c: Correct. ALB has approximately 400 milliseconds of latency due to Layer 7 processing.
exp.d: Incorrect. 1000ms would be excessively high.

q: Which AWS service can be integrated with ALB to protect against common web exploits?

exp.a: Incorrect. AWS Shield protects against DDoS attacks but WAF is specifically for web exploits.
exp.b: Correct. AWS WAF can be directly attached to an ALB to protect against common web exploits like SQL injection, XSS, and to create custom rules.
exp.c: Incorrect. GuardDuty is a threat detection service, not a web firewall.
exp.d: Incorrect. Inspector is a vulnerability assessment service.

q: What happens during a scale-out event in an Auto Scaling Group?

opts.b: New instances are launched to increase capacity

exp.a: Incorrect. Terminating instances is a scale-in event.
exp.b: Correct. Scale-out means adding (launching) new instances to handle increased demand.
exp.c: Incorrect. Instance type changes are not part of scale-out in ASG.
exp.d: Incorrect. EBS volume expansion is unrelated to ASG scaling.

q: What happens during a scale-in event in an Auto Scaling Group?

opts.b: Instances are terminated to decrease capacity
opts.c: Instances are stopped but not terminated
opts.d: Instances are moved to another region

exp.a: Incorrect. Adding instances is a scale-out event.
exp.b: Correct. Scale-in means terminating instances to reduce capacity when demand decreases.
exp.c: Incorrect. ASG terminates instances during scale-in, not just stops them.
exp.d: Incorrect. ASG does not move instances between regions.

q: Which of the following is NOT a valid target type for an NLB target group?

exp.a: Incorrect. EC2 instances are valid NLB targets.
exp.b: Incorrect. IP addresses are valid NLB targets.
exp.c: Correct. Lambda functions are NOT supported as targets for NLB. Lambda functions are supported only by ALB.
exp.d: Incorrect. ALB can be a target behind NLB (to get static IPs with ALB features).

q: What is the maximum number of Availability Zones an ELB can span within a region?

exp.a: Incorrect. ELB can span more than 2 AZs.
exp.b: Incorrect. ELB is not limited to 3 AZs.
exp.c: Correct. An ELB can span all Availability Zones within a region (the number varies by region).
exp.d: Incorrect. The limit depends on the number of AZs in the region, which can be more or less than 5.

q: What is the maximum deregistration delay (connection draining) that can be configured?

exp.a: Incorrect. 300 seconds is the default, not the maximum.
exp.b: Incorrect. 600 seconds is not the maximum.
exp.c: Incorrect. 1800 seconds is not the maximum.
exp.d: Correct. The maximum deregistration delay can be set up to 3600 seconds (1 hour). The range is 0-3600 seconds.

q: Which CloudWatch metric for ASG tracks the number of instances that the ASG is managing?

exp.a: Incorrect. GroupDesiredCapacity shows the desired number of instances, not the actual number in service.
exp.b: Correct. GroupInServiceInstances represents the number of instances currently running and in service within the ASG.
exp.c: Incorrect. GroupTotalInstances includes all instances in all states.
exp.d: Incorrect. GroupPendingInstances shows instances being launched but not yet in service.

q: What is a Launch Template in AWS?

opts.a: A template for creating S3 buckets
opts.b: A configuration template that specifies instance configuration (AMI, instance type, key pair, security groups, etc.) for ASG

exp.a: Incorrect. S3 bucket creation does not use launch templates.
exp.b: Correct. A Launch Template defines the configuration for EC2 instances including AMI ID, instance type, key pair, security groups, user data, and more. ASG uses it to launch new instances.
exp.c: Incorrect. VPC creation does not use launch templates.
exp.d: Incorrect. CloudFormation uses its own template format (JSON/YAML).

q: What is the difference between Launch Templates and Launch Configurations?

opts.a: They are exactly the same thing
opts.b: Launch Templates support versioning and are newer; Launch Configurations are legacy and do not support versioning
opts.c: Launch Configurations support versioning but Launch Templates do not
opts.d: Launch Configurations work with ALB but Launch Templates do not

exp.a: Incorrect. They have different capabilities.
exp.b: Correct. Launch Templates are newer, support versioning, can use mixed instance types/purchase options, and are recommended by AWS. Launch Configurations are legacy and cannot be modified after creation.
exp.c: Incorrect. It is the opposite — Launch Templates support versioning.
exp.d: Incorrect. Both can work with any ELB type.
